question: Explain virtual memory and why operating systems use it instead of letting programs access physical memory directly.

key_points: Virtual memory gives each process its own private address space, isolated from other processes — a process can't accidentally (or maliciously) read/write another process's memory
Allows a process to use more memory than physically available RAM, by keeping less-used pages on disk (swap/page file) and loading them back in on demand (paging)

Simplifies programming: each process can assume it has a contiguous, large address space starting from a fixed address, without needing to coordinate with other processes about which physical addresses are free
The OS/MMU (memory management unit) translates virtual addresses to physical addresses transparently via page tables, with a page fault triggered when an accessed page isn't currently in physical RAM
reference_solution.sample_answer: Virtual memory gives every process the illusion of its own private, contiguous address space, completely isolated from other processes — so a bug or malicious code in one process can't directly read or corrupt another process's memory, since it only ever sees virtual addresses, which are translated to real physical addresses by the memory management unit hardware, guided by page tables the OS maintains. It also lets a process use more memory than is physically installed, by keeping less-frequently-used memory pages out on disk in swap space and bringing them back into physical RAM on demand when accessed — triggering what's called a page fault if the needed page isn't currently resident in RAM. This also greatly simplifies programming, since a process can assume it has a large, contiguous address space starting from a predictable address, without needing to know or negotiate which actual physical memory addresses happen to be free at that moment.

follow_up_hint: Ask what happens, step by step, when a program accesses a virtual address whose page isn't currently in physical RAM (a page fault).

question: Explain the difference between preemptive and cooperative multitasking, and name a common CPU scheduling algorithm.

key_points: Cooperative multitasking: a running process/thread voluntarily yields control back to the scheduler; a misbehaving process that never yields can freeze the whole system

Preemptive multitasking: the OS can forcibly interrupt a running process (via a timer interrupt) and switch to another, regardless of whether the process 'wants' to yield — this is what virtually all modern OSes use

Common scheduling algorithms: Round Robin (each process gets a fixed time slice in rotation, fair and simple), Shortest Job First (minimizes average wait time but requires knowing job length upfront), Priority scheduling (higher-priority processes run first, with care needed to avoid starving low-priority ones)
Explains preemption is essential for responsiveness/fairness in a general-purpose multi-user OS
reference_solution.sample_answer: In cooperative multitasking, a running process voluntarily yields control back to the scheduler at some point; the risk is a poorly behaved or buggy process that never yields can freeze the entire system, since nothing can forcibly take control back. Preemptive multitasking, which virtually all modern general-purpose operating systems use, lets the OS forcibly interrupt a running process via a hardware timer interrupt and switch to a different one, regardless of whether the current process wants to give up control, which is essential for fairness and responsiveness. A common scheduling algorithm is Round Robin, where each process gets a fixed time slice in rotation, which is simple and fair; other examples include Shortest Job First, which minimizes average wait time but requires knowing job length upfront, and Priority scheduling, where higher-priority processes run first, though that needs safeguards like priority aging to avoid permanently starving lower-priority processes.

follow_up_hint: Ask what 'priority inversion' is and how it can cause a high-priority task to be effectively blocked by a low-priority one.

question: What is a context switch, and why does it have a real performance cost?

key_points: A context switch is the CPU saving the complete state (registers, program counter, stack pointer) of the currently running process/thread, and loading the saved state of a different one to resume it
Cost: directly, the CPU cycles spent saving/restoring this state, and the OS scheduler's own bookkeeping overhead

Indirect cost, often larger: cache/TLB pollution — the new process's working set isn't in the CPU cache or TLB (translation lookaside buffer) yet, so it runs slower initially until those warm back up ('cold cache' effect)
Explains this is why having too many runnable threads/processes competing for a limited number of CPU cores (excessive context switching) can hurt overall throughput, not just per-process latency
reference_solution.sample_answer: A context switch is when the CPU saves the complete state of the currently running process or thread — its registers, program counter, stack pointer — and loads the previously saved state of a different process or thread to resume running it. The direct cost is the CPU cycles spent actually saving and restoring all that state plus the scheduler's own bookkeeping to decide what runs next, but there's often a larger indirect cost: the CPU's cache and TLB were 'warm' with the previous process's data and address translations, and the newly scheduled process starts with a cold cache, running slower initially until its own working set gets loaded back in. This is exactly why having far more runnable threads than available CPU cores, causing excessive context switching, can actually hurt total system throughput, not just add latency to any individual process — the CPU spends a meaningful fraction of its time switching rather than doing useful work.

follow_up_hint: Ask why a context switch between two threads of the SAME process is typically cheaper than a context switch between two different processes.
